answer.rationale: The 18% cost mandate is severe and the 14-day renewal window is tight. Renegotiation has proven effective in memory_c4 (recovered real margin through benchmarking) and memory_c6 shows multi-year commitments can unlock volume pricing without narrowing scope. Renewing incumbent (memory_c1) maintains stability but does not address the cost mandate. Switching primary vendor (memory_c2) worked well but carries migration risk at 94% line utilization. Adding a second source addresses resilience but not cost pressure directly. Deferring risks contract lapse with no coverage. Verifying memory_c4 (renegotiation success) and memory_c2 (vendor switch execution) will confirm whether aggressive renegotiation is realistic given tight timeline, or whether a switch is operationally feasible at current utilization. A negotiation-first posture leverages the incumbent relationship and integration stability while forcing cost recalibration against market benchmarks and the hard 18% target. This preserves the option to escalate to a switch if negotiation fails, and preserves budget flexibility if terms cannot be met. The assembly line buffer risk is real and renegotiation minimizes migration disruption.
